contributions.text_english: Can I support the Member in his questions on this topic, First Minister? We know that many older people at the moment are struggling with the cost of living, and particularly with the impact of a fixed income on many older people in our communities. We also know that, historically, people have been able to access advice services in their communities through organisations such as Citizens Advice and other fantastic organisations like that, who can support our older people to ensure that they are making the best use of any welfare support available to them and other types of support as well. So, I wonder, First Minister, if you're able to outline how you see those types of services in the future and what support the Welsh Government can give to organisations like the citizens advice bureaux to ensure that that advice is available to them in a timely way, and in an accessible way as well? contributions.text_english:
Thank you for your response, Cabinet Minister. Before the recess, I was pleased to be able to highlight, in this Chamber, that the championships were taking place in north Wales over the summer. And it was a huge success, hosted at four different locations across north Wales, including the very own Racecourse ground in my own constituency of Fflint Wrecsam.

But just before the tournament ended, the four chief medical officers of Wales, England, Scotland and Northern Ireland came together to release a new physical activity guidelines report that encourages children and young people to engage in 60 minutes per day of physical activity, such as sports. And I'm sure you'd agree that engaging in that physical activity benefits our physical and mental health and can certainly relieve pressures in our NHS, and it's just better for people in the long run. So, I wonder how you see your role, in working with the Minister responsible for our health services, to ensure that children are encouraged to take part in sports activities. And I wonder also whether you reflect on the Member's Bill that I raised in this Senedd last term, which was seeking to encourage more young people to engage in outdoor activities, and whether there's any opportunity to review any of the work that took place in the last Senedd term on outdoor activities for children in schools.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english:
Well, thank you for your response, Cabinet Minister. Last week, the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy released a written statement informing Members that the Welsh Government is going to write off £684,000 in unpaid rent owed by P.V. France Limited, a significant amount of taxpayers' money. There may be some specific reasons why that business went into difficulty, but what concerns me is how that debt of nearly £700,000 was allowed to reach such an extraordinary level in the first place. The Welsh Government, we understand, agreed to multiple payment plans, yet the arrears continued to build time after time. The company eventually entered administration, was dissolved, and now that money, nearly £700,000, seemingly cannot be recovered. 

At a time when we're being told that the public finances are incredibly tight, as I'm sure they are, how can the Government justify allowing almost £700,000 of taxpayers' money to be lost in this way? And as the Minister responsible for holding those purse strings, how will you prevent this from happening again in the future?

contributions.item_title_en: 4. 90-second Statements
contributions.text_english:
On Saturday, I was pleased to attend the official launch of the Football Museum of Wales and Wrexham Museum. As a member for Fflint Wrecsam, it was a real pleasure to be part of such an important occasion for the area and to join with colleagues in seeing the Cabinet Minister cut the ribbon on the museum.

The launch was a fantastic opportunity to celebrate the heritage of Wrexham and the history of Welsh football, and to see the new galleries and the stories they have to tell. I'm sure many of us agree that football is such an important part of communities across Wales. It brings people together, sometimes drives them apart, but creates shared opportunities and is a huge part of our national identity. The Football Museum of Wales provides a fantastic opportunity to preserve that history and share it with future generations.

The Wrexham Museum also plays an important role in celebrating the city, its people and its heritage. I was particularly pleased to meet those involved in making these museums a reality and to see the pride and enthusiasm surrounding the launch. These museums have huge potential to attract visitors, support the local economy and showcase Wrexham to people from across Wales and beyond. I hope the Welsh Government will recognise that potential and continue to work with and support both museums as they establish themselves and grow. They are important cultural assets for Wrexham and for Wales and deserve every opportunity to succeed.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Questions to the First Minister
contributions.text_english:
Thank you for your response, First Minister, but the issues you've outlined are part of the reason why Members in this place and the public at large are so frustrated with your obsessive pursuit of independence when what you should be doing is focusing on these issues in the classrooms to support our children for the best outcomes possible. Wales is falling behind every other UK nation in maths, reading and science, with the gap particularly stark when compared with England. You rightfully want to work with other countries and co-operate and learn from them. Why don't you learn from England as to how they are doing so well with their education outcomes compared with our children here in Wales?

If we're serious about driving up those standards, we have to also address what is happening in our classrooms. We've heard time and time again from Estyn and the teaching unions as to poor behaviour as an issue in our classrooms. We've been clear that teachers need to be properly supported, schools need a stronger approach to discipline, so that teachers can teach and pupils can learn without unnecessary disruption. Given these disappointing PISA results, First Minister, will you accept that improving discipline, supporting teachers and restoring high expectations in our classrooms must be at the heart of any plan to raise educational standards?

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
contributions.text_english:
Cabinet Minister, thank you for your statement today. I do share some of the concerns raised by our Reform colleague in terms of the way in which this information has been disseminated to Members of the Senedd. I think it is right and proper that in the vast majority of instances, information is shared in this Chamber first before being released to the press, just to show some respect to the Chamber itself and the Members within it.

But in terms of the meat of this statement, I certainly welcome the direction of travel from the Government on this and recognise that business rates represent a significant cost for businesses across Wales at a time when many are already under considerable pressures. Cabinet Minister, you'll be aware that our high streets have been struggling to adapt to changing consumer behaviour and the continued growth of online retail. The Welsh Conservatives have consistently argued that the tax burden on those businesses is far too high. We also need to be honest about the wider pressures that businesses are facing, dealing with taxation of all types alongside employee pressures and rising energy costs. Of course, business rates are only one part of a wider cost of doing business.

Colleagues have already raised a couple of questions I was interested in. I will point to three issues and questions, though. Respectfully, Cabinet Minister, I'm not sure if you fully responded to Huw Thomas's question, particularly around the cliff edge. You acknowledged it in your response, but, of course, there has potentially been the introduction of a new cliff edge here. I wonder what assurances you can give those businesses that they won't feel the pain of that, potentially, and that there may be some tapering that could take place so businesses aren't falling foul one way or the other. What confidence can you give to businesses that that is properly understood and recognised in terms of a potential tapering of this relief beyond that £51,000? A broader discussion you mentioned in regard to business rates, I think, does need to take place. I'd expect Welsh Government to lead on that.

There was one specific issue I'd be grateful for you to consider in this discussion, and that's one around the particular challenges faced by businesses who are just starting out. Business rates will ordinarily apply as soon as they start up, meaning firms can face a tax bill very soon after opening their doors without necessarily generating real income at that point. I wonder what consideration you might give to our proposal for business rate free periods for new retail businesses and others on the high street to give those entrepreneurs the opportunity to establish themselves before facing this additional cost.

Another consideration on which I'd be interested in your response is the role of local authorities in business rates. Of course, many people think that councils set those business rates, but they merely collect them on behalf of the Welsh Government. But I wonder if there's an opportunity to incentivise our local authorities by allowing them to retain an element of any non-domestic rates growth in their area, to allow our councils to invest in our town centres or incentivise our councils perhaps to invest in those town centres more than they currently do.

Finally, Minister, I'm interested—and it's back to this particular announcement today—in how it's going to impact businesses that offer mixed services. In my own constituency, Banana Ben's play centre and cafe may be impacted by this. They've been refused food and drink hospitality rate relief in the past, despite food and drink accounting for 60 per cent of their floor space and 61 per cent of their turnover. Companies House classify it as an unlicensed restaurant and cafe. The business provides indoor play alongside food and drink for families, and the two, of course, are not mutually exclusive, yet it will not, it seems, qualify for the equivalent relief. Businesses of a similar nature in England absolutely do. So, I wonder whether you could respond to that and what you might seek to do to address this disparity to ensure that Welsh businesses are not disadvantaged simply because they operate in Wales, perhaps offering more than one service to their customers. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Review of Higher Education
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Apologies for my slight lapse in concentration, things seem to be more lively outside the Chamber today than they have been, perhaps, inside it.

Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement. Tertiary education is, of course, crucial in developing the skills and knowledge that our economy needs now and in the future, and the stakes for the higher education review could hardly be higher at this stage. And the many external reviews of Welsh higher education over recent decades, in my view, have failed to secure the long-term sustainability of the sector and have instead contributed to a cycle of managed decline.

But on this review specifically, you'll be aware, Cabinet Minister, that in Scotland when Ministers have sought to work with universities to develop solutions and secure their commitments to change, before holding them to account for delivery, there's been that close working relationship with those universities. So, I wonder how you will ensure and give assurances to our universities here in Wales that you'll be adopting a similar approach, working seriously with those universities as partners in developing and implementing these reforms, of course within the context of the independent panel that you're seeking to or you will be setting up.

There's already been mention of the central role that universities play in our economy and our growth in the future. We welcome the review's commitment to look at the role that alternative pathways, such as colleges and degree apprenticeships, should play in a wider education landscape. Of course, colleges can provide flexible modes of delivery and be more accessible to learners, and we know the increasing importance of a degree apprenticeship. So, will you direct the review to look specifically at what barriers there are in Wales to prevent our young people from accessing some of those alternative pathways that colleagues have already mentioned, those alternative pathways to higher education.

Within that context of economic growth, universities are important engines of place-based economic growth as well, not just the institution on its own. There are great examples of universities working closely in partnership with colleges and local industry to respond to the skills that are needed. Now, FE is not covered in the review, so how will you make sure there's a joined-up approach to meeting place-based skills requirements and opportunities across the tertiary systems? I appreciate that HE does need to be reviewed, but the context of their place is really important, particularly in a place like Wales.

Deputy Minister, in your terms of reference, you state that the scale and urgency of pressures on universities mean that the underlying funding sustainability of Welsh universities and the Welsh student support system must now be addressed. There's a real sense of urgency in your statements there, but the timeline that you're looking at is looking to make changes in the 2028-29 academic year. That's two years away. It doesn't really feel that urgent, quite frankly. Welsh students starting university in September will be entering the final year of their courses by the time any changes come in. Could you confirm whether you think that a two-year wait for this reform is acceptable to students, universities and businesses under pressure right now?

I just want to follow up on a comment that my colleague Lynne Neagle raised as well, Minister, in relation to this ambition of students seeking an education where it's best for them. Wales is already home to world-class universities. For many students, though, looking elsewhere in the UK or abroad is simply what's best for them and their future pathway. That should be a choice that is equally available to them. Higher education should allow our students to aspire to become the best that they can be, to be supported. They don't want to feel hemmed in by Wales-specific Government support or not. So, will you, on the floor of the Senedd today, commit to not holding back those Welsh student aspirations to study wherever is best for them? Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language: The Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Plan
contributions.text_english:
Cabinet Minister, I'm sure you'd be fascinated to hear that I had a very interesting start to my day today, because I had the privilege of formally welcoming Logos Hope to Cardiff Bay, the ship that's docked here for three weeks. I would encourage all Members of the Chamber to take a visit, if you get a chance. It's the world's largest floating book fair. Now, I'm not sure how many floating book fairs there are, but this is the biggest one in the world. On that ship, there are around 350 volunteers of 50 different nationalities going around the world supporting children particularly with their literacy and education, and they do an incredible job.

But the reason I mention it now is that, in one of the contributions by the managing director on the ship today, he invoked the spirit of Griffith Jones and pointed out the literacy heritage that we have here in Wales and, of course, his work on the circulating schools in the eighteenth century, and the global reputation. There are over 50 nationalities on this ship and they recognise the heritage we have here in Wales around literacy in particular. It struck me, as I sat there, where we, sadly, find ourselves at the moment. You opened your statement by pointing to the fact that it's not all about PISA, but clearly the OECD are pointing to our downward trend at the moment in particular on reading and maths, and I know it's a wake-up call for you, but, in particular, it's a concern that parents have of children in schools and they recognise that far too many children are leaving school without the strong foundations that they need.

So, I wonder, as my first question to you, after years of promises to raise standards—and parents have heard this before and teachers have heard this before—what confidence can you give to parents and teachers that this plan will finally deliver the improvement that they've been waiting for? And let me point out, Cabinet Minister, the things that I am really supportive of on this here, in particular the focus on the nought-16 approach, I think that's very helpful; literacy and numeracy don't suddenly start when a child walks through the school gates, and we need to understand where children are starting from, track that progress and identify where support is needed before problems become entrenched. That goes back to that point around the parental involvement. I was really pleased to see, in your actual plan, foundation 1, which is the role of parents and carers, and let me encourage you to push as strongly as possible in that area, because we know the huge difference that good parenting and support at home can make to those children in their first few years. I also welcome the proposed year 6 indicator. If a child is struggling with reading and numeracy at the end of primary school, the secondary school needs to know that as best as possible, but good information sharing can make a real difference to that transition and to the support that children receive. So, I wonder if you would outline more clearly how the Welsh Government will ensure that this information actually leads to earlier and better support.

I do have some concerns, as I'm sure you'd expect, and some of those are around how this works in practice. I think colleagues have already mentioned the existing workload that teachers have, and I know you've responded to some of that. They don't want more paperwork, they don't want more bureaucracy, they don't want more sand in the system; they want this to work as smoothly as possible. So, I wonder, in your response to me, if you can give those reassurances that you recognise that again, and that, whilst we're asking schools to set ambitious targets, they'll be given the resources, training and support to be able to achieve this.

I also noticed in the opening of your plan document, Cabinet Minister, that you point out, and I'll quote here, that:

'A sustained period of reform has taken its toll, and literacy and numeracy have been lost in the noise.'

You go on, though, to say that the new plan is deliberate—I can't say the word; my literacy skills need to be improved—

'deliberately iterative and will be subject to ongoing review and evaluation'.

Now, those two things, perhaps, seem to fight each other, and I wonder what assurances you can give to our schools that—. You pointed out that all this reform has taken a lot of energy in the system, but then go on to say that they'll be subject to ongoing review and evaluation. So, I think schools would want to know how are you going to get that tension right. How are you going to ensure that, whilst those reviews are important, actually, they need to be getting on with the job in hand?

I believe time is up, Deputy Presiding Officer, so I look forward to the response, but perhaps I have one moment. We cannot, of course, decouple literacy and numeracy outcomes from some basic expectations in schools. I questioned the First Minister earlier around how we're going to address classroom behaviours, because, for children to gain those literacy and numeracy skills, they need to be in the best place possible in the classroom around behaviours as well. So, I'd appreciate any response on that as well. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Welsh Conservatives Debate: Deposit-return scheme
contributions.text_english:
In answer to previous speakers' challenge back to the Conservatives a moment ago, the fundamental issue here is the divergence away from the rest of the UK and the complexity that creates in the system, increasing the cost, increasing the pressures for businesses and, ultimately, for consumers, who are the ones who will pay the literal cost of this at the end.

As a Member for the Fflint Wrecsam constituency, I see every day how interconnected our communities are here in the UK. People are constantly moving between England and Wales to work, shop and visit family, with businesses trading seamlessly across that border. What they need is that certainty and consistency, not that divergence and additional bureaucracy for bureaucracy's sake. That's why, as Janet Finch-Saunders outlined in her opening, we've consistently supported a fully aligned, cross-nation, four-nation, deposit-return scheme approach.

It's also the position of the Welsh Beer and Pub Association, which has warned that different schemes across the UK will create unnecessary complexity and, ultimately, additional costs. The association has called for a fully aligned, four-nation approach, which would mean excluding glass from the scheme. Glass would create unnecessary complexity and additional costs for producers, retailers—and, again, let's not forget those consumers, who are the ones that would be paying for this through their purchases. Those costs could ultimately lead to higher prices, reduce consumer choice as some brands will reconsider the Welsh market, and greater pressure on smaller Welsh businesses. Again, the previous Labour speaker talked about the opportunities around green growth, but what hasn't been acknowledged is the potential losses because of the higher costs of dealing with this proposed scheme.

The Association of Convenience Stores has raised similar concerns. We'd all share the feeling that local shops are at the heart of communities across Wales, particularly in our rural areas. They'd play a vital role in the success of any deposit-return scheme. Yet, many convenience stores simply do not have the space to accommodate glass returns, and the specialist reverse vending machines required are significantly more expensive. Especially at a time when many independent retailers are already under pressure, this is a very serious concern for them. The inclusion of glass is not simply an environmental question, it's a practical one. We should ask whether it's the right way to achieve our environmental ambitions, without placing unnecessary burdens on retailers, producers, and importantly, again, consumers.

It's already been mentioned in this debate, Deputy Presiding Officer, the question of readiness. With the scheme due to launch in October 2027, a little over a year away, businesses seem to lack the certainty they need. The Association of Convenience Stores, as we've already heard, has urged the Welsh Government to appoint the deposit management organisation as soon as possible so those retailers can invest, adapt their operations and train staff appropriately. Without that certainty, the October 2027 deadline will become increasingly difficult to achieve. I know the Cabinet Minister wants to, perhaps, speak to that point specifically in his response, and I look forward to hearing from him on that.

I also think the Cabinet Minister does get this issue. I know that he sees the problem that businesses are facing at the moment with this and the issues that divergence will create. I ask the Cabinet Minister to reflect on what he, I'm sure, feels in his heart of hearts are the issues this is going to cause, and actually reflect on the costs it's going to cause to businesses. Your Plaid Cymru Government here often talked in their campaign that they wanted the economy at the heart of this new Plaid Cymru Government. So, listen to what businesses are telling you on this scheme at the moment, listen to their concerns and align with the rest of the UK.

So, I ask the Cabinet Minister specifically: will the Welsh Government commit to working with other UK nations to deliver a truly interoperable deposit-return scheme? Will you consider that the inclusion of glass at launch risks increasing costs for Welsh businesses and consumers? Will you acknowledge that? And will you urgently appoint a deposit management organisation so that businesses have the certainty they need to prepare?

Deputy Presiding Officer, I will wrap up by saying that environmental ambition and economic common sense should go hand in hand. We can deliver a successful deposit-return scheme, but only if it is practical, affordable and aligned with the rest of the UK. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Deputy First Minister and Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality: Update on Early Years Childcare and Play
contributions.text_english:
I'd like to, first of all, thank the Cabinet Minister for today's statement and for the advance notice of it that she provided to Members. Absolutely, every parent and carer wants the best start for their child, but for too many families the cost of childcare is making that much harder. We all know parents who are weighing up whether it's even worth returning to work because those childcare costs take up such a large proportion of their income, and, as the Cabinet Minister outlined, in some cases, those costs are higher than rent, mortgages or other headline costs.

Of course, the challenge that we're discussing today also feeds into this broader issue of falling birth rates and the challenge that that's going to present to us as a nation in the years to come. That's why we, on these benches, welcome any genuine attempt to make childcare more affordable and more accessible to parents. But I guess the question in this place today is whether what's being discussed can actually be delivered. Because, of course, warm words, on their own, aren't enough.

To begin with, we believe that the childcare system in its current form is far too complex, especially for parents to navigate and understand what they are entitled to, and I acknowledge the Cabinet Minister's reference to that in her statement here today. We believe that one of the first things that the Welsh Government should be looking at is how to streamline and simplify childcare funding so that parents in particular can easily understand what support is available to them so that they can properly plan for the future. So, I'd be interested to know, Cabinet Minister, what actions you'll be taking to engage with parents and carers to ensure that any unnecessary complexity is taken out of the system for them.

Secondly, the announcement of the £55 million investment is, of course, welcome. However, families and providers need greater clarity about how this funding will, exactly, be used—how many additional children will benefit—and certainty that it will reach those who need it most. On the funding point, I do want to pick up on the comments made by my colleague in Fflint Wrecsam, who was absolutely right to call out this midpoint estimate of £375 million. I believe, in your response, you suggested that there is a range there, of course, and the maximum could be up to a £500 million cost. That is, of course, significantly higher than initially expected from your manifesto, so I'm interested to understand how you're planning to manage that potential cost. I appreciate it's not necessarily what the cost will be, but how are you managing to mitigate any unnecessary escalation in costs?

I'm interested also, Cabinet Minister, in the response you gave to our Labour colleague on the broader support services for families and for children, and how you'll be working with health services to ensure that holistic support is available and the capacity is there in those health services to deliver on that ambition that you mentioned in your response to Lynne Neagle.

I also want to recognise the pressures that childcare providers are under, as colleagues have done already. We know that these are often small businesses delivering an essential service, often on very limited margins. We know that they're often struggling with rising costs, recruitment challenges and tight budgets. You have already acknowledged the necessity of a workforce plan and you've outlined that the plan will come forward in the autumn. I'm interested to understand how you expect to work with skills providers to ensure that the workforce is available quickly, because you will know, of course, that those skills take years to be in place, and you want to move at pace on this issue.

I also welcome the updated national minimum standards. Every child deserves a safe environment where they can learn, develop and enjoy being a child. Higher standards matter, but so does ensuring providers have the support and resources to meet them. Would you be able to explain what support will be available to help settings implement these new standards?

Finally, Cabinet Minister, you may have noted that in our manifesto we talked about an idea around a grandparent payment scheme or a nominated family payment scheme to recognise the role of the wider family in bringing up children. You say that it takes a village to bring up a child. I wonder what consideration you’ve given to a scheme similar to that, where a nominated family member is able to be supported to support bringing a child up, rather than, perhaps, necessarily, that money always going to a childcare provider setting. At the end of the day, parents want childcare that is safe, affordable and reliable. Providers want a system that is properly funded, sustainable and workable. Those are the priorities that we should all be focused on. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Skills and Tertiary Education: Priorities for Skills and Tertiary Education
contributions.text_english:
I thank the Deputy Minister for today's statement and the advance notice of it as well. We absolutely agree—skills and tertiary education are central to Wales's future. We want to grow our economy and create opportunities with a skills system that's ambitious, flexible and responsive to employers' and businesses' needs. And while we welcome the focus on understanding future skills requirements and bringing together employers, colleges and universities, Deputy Minister, you will know that businesses are already facing skills shortages and cannot wait for years for action to take place. So, I echo comments made from across the Chamber, because what those businesses need to know is not necessarily what the skills plan is for future years, but what's going to happen now to plug the gaps that they are experiencing. Because, frankly, we've heard strategies and reviews before; employers are desperate for action today. And I can give you a quick example.

I recently met with the Electrical Contractors Association, who highlighted to me the shortage of skilled electricians. Back in 2015, there were 13,500 electricians here in Wales; that number is now 7,600, so nearly half the number of electricians in Wales that we had just over 10 years ago. And you will know, Deputy Minister, the need for electrical contract work is going to expand, as that's a huge part of our economy in the future. So, an example there of the number of people in a skilled workforce being nearly halved over a 10-year period. Businesses and employers want to know what you are doing now to make sure those gaps are being plugged.

That links specifically, also, to apprenticeships. I've heard your comments on the junior apprenticeships, but I think part of the problem at the moment, and the challenge at the moment, in particular for small businesses, is making the system as simple as possible, removing unnecessary bureaucracy and improving the funding, so that those businesses can access those apprenticeships and support those apprenticeships in the future. We, as Welsh Conservatives, in our manifesto, were keen to see more than 100,000 apprenticeships delivered over this Senedd term. I'm not sure if there's a target coming from Welsh Government at the moment; I'd be interested to hear your thoughts on that. But I guess the question is, Deputy Minister: how will you be looking to make apprenticeships easier to access, more attractive to learners, and ensure that Wales is developing the skilled workforce our economy requires with apprenticeships in mind?

We certainly welcome the commitment to increase funding for Welsh-medium education and training, particularly within apprenticeships as well. Those Welsh-medium skills are important across many sectors, but I wonder if you could outline how this commitment will be funded and delivered.

You mentioned our universities, of course, higher education, who are facing significant pressures. Representatives from the sector have raised concerns about those financial challenges, job losses and long-term sustainability. We know that more than 1,000 university jobs have been lost across Wales in the past year alone, while falling international student numbers and demographic changes are creating further uncertainty. We welcome the review of university funding, but you'll know that it must deliver practical solutions, not just another consultation.

Deputy Minister, you've spoken prior to this statement of the possibility of university mergers, but there's little clarity about what this actually means. Of course, forced mergers would be a major undertaking and may not address the underlying problems in universities. So, I wonder, in your response, if you could clarify what role you see mergers playing, whether there are particular models you're considering, and whether any options are off the table at this stage.

Finally, Deputy Minister, skills are not just about young people entering work, as you would acknowledge. Wales must become a lifelong learning nation where adults can retrain, upskill and adapt throughout their careers. So, I wonder if you could expand further on what the Welsh Government is doing to ensure adults across Wales have access to flexible learning opportunities that will enable them to gain new skills and qualifications. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 9. Debate: The First Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'm pleased to speak in this debate today on behalf of the Finance Committee. We had the privilege of scrutinising the first supplementary budget on 9 July and our report makes 22 recommendations. Today, I will focus on some of our key recommendations. 

As we've heard, the supplementary budget that the committee scrutinised included £246 million of unallocated resource funding, which the Cabinet Minister said reflects substantial in-year pressures, particularly within the NHS. We recognise that there is always some uncertainty at this stage of the financial year and that Governments need a degree of flexibility to respond to emerging pressures, but the level of unallocated funding is considerably higher than in recent supplementary budgets. The committee noted that the average over the last four years has been £62 million and it's currently around four times higher than the average of the last four years. We want to better understand what pressures remain across Government and how those pressures differ from the normal challenges of managing a budget through the financial year.

Turning to the management of NHS finances, this supplementary budget includes a £100 million allocation to tackle NHS waiting lists. The committee supports the Government's ambition to move beyond short-term interventions and deliver sustained improvement in NHS performance. And we heard the Cabinet Minister wants to focus on longer term outcomes rather than short-term monthly performance measures. We heard that the NHS is currently facing financial pressures of more than £300 million this year and that discussions with health boards are ongoing before further funding decisions are taken. However, what we did not hear in sufficient detail is how the approach of this Government differs from previous approaches that have also relied on significant in-year NHS allocation. That is why we asked the Cabinet Minister to detail the accountability mechanisms and measures in place to ensure the £100 million for reductions in waiting lists is used effectively, and to explain the practical differences between the previous approaches to NHS funding and the new Government's approach. We want to understand how these investments will drive sustainable improvement rather than short-term recovery measures.

Moving on to the allocation of funding arising from the one-off special educational needs and disabilities consequential. Firstly, we recognise that the principle that Barnett consequentials do not have to be spent in the same way as funding allocated in England is an important principle. We also recognise the very real pressures facing additional learning needs services across Wales in the here and now. The Cabinet Minister told us that this one-off consequential has been absorbed into wider budget management. That inevitably raises questions about sustainability in other areas. We therefore ask her to explain how allocations enabled by this one-off consequential will be managed in future years, when that funding is no longer available. The Cabinet Minister told us the Government wants to work with local government and develop a more sustainable model for additional learning needs provision, recognising the significant pressure in the system. That is why we're seeking greater clarity on both the scale of the challenge and the Government's plan to manage these pressures.

The committee noted the Government's plans to expand funded childcare. The supplementary budget includes £55 million to accelerate the roll-out of funded childcare for two-year-olds and to support the wider expansion of the childcare offer. We asked the Cabinet Minister to confirm how many places the £55 million allocation will support, what outcomes are expected from the funding and how those outcomes will be monitored and reported.

We will now turn to capital budgets. The Government has chosen to allocate virtually all available capital funding at this stage of the year. We understand the rationale and recognise the benefits of allocating capital funding early to facilitate delivery and support economic activity, however, that approach also leaves limited flexibility should circumstances change. We're particularly concerned by reports that UK Government decisions associated with defence investment could have implications for Welsh capital budgets. We asked the Cabinet Minister to provide an assessment of the implications of the UK Government's defence investment plan and any consequences for Welsh Government capital budgets.

Too often, debate focuses solely on the amounts of money being spent; the Finance Committee understands that what matters most is what that money delivers. We look forward to the Cabinet Minister's response and to continue our scrutiny of these issues as the financial year progresses. Diolch, Lywydd.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Member’s Legislative Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): A Bill on corporate parenting
contributions.text_english:
The Welsh Conservatives want to begin by recognising the importance of the proposal in front of us today, and commend the Member for bringing it forward. I had the privilege, Deputy Presiding Officer, of serving on a fostering panel for nearly 10 years in a previous role, and it gives you a real insight as to the importance of the work that takes place in local authorities currently.

Of course, corporate parenting, at its best, is about the state acting, when required, as a responsible parent should, with consistency, care, attention, love, compassion and a genuine focus on that child's long-term future—all the things that a birth parent should do, but in all areas. It is reflected in the motion in front of us today. It's quite striking that this seems to be required to take place. I think many people, our constituents, would assume that this role of corporate parenting is already embedded within public bodies across Wales. I think they would be surprised to see a motion like this having to be tabled here today. So, I certainly commend the Member for bringing it forward.

I also want to acknowledge the positive role of the 2026 legislation referenced at a UK level, affecting young people in England, the recognition of that as improving those life chances of care-experienced children. And it requires a whole-system approach. It's absolutely right that Wales now considers how best to achieve the same ambition. If stronger corporate parenting responsibilities across public bodies are helping those children in England, then why should we expect anything less for children here in Wales? I absolutely support the principle that every part of the public sector should play its part in improving outcomes for looked-after children and care leavers. I think it's the very least that people would expect.

I just want to touch on a point—I appreciate time really is flying for this matter today; it's a 30-minute debate for such an important item today. I'm not sure whether that's usual for Members' legislative proposals, but it does feel like quite a tight timescale, because, whilst I hope there's support for this legislation in this place today, there's also a conversation needed around the implementation of this as well. Because we know public services are stretched at the moment, and it's essential that any new duties are backed by resources, workforce capacity and clear guidance to make it meaningful in practice as well. So, I'd be interested to hear the Government's views on that. Because we cannot simply place new statutory responsibilities on already stretched services and expect better outcomes without giving them the tools to succeed. I think we've seen that happen time and time again when things are agreed in this place, when the resources don't follow to enable things to be enacted fully and properly.

So, I will conclude, Deputy Presiding Officer, by saying that we will support this legislative proposal. We're also really keen to engage constructively, as it progresses, to ensure that these duties are matched by the resources and workforce capacity needed to make it effective as well. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Trauma and Adverse Childhood Experience (ACE)
contributions.text_english:
I'm very pleased to be able to support this motion here today, and certainly grateful to the Member for tabling it, and to everybody so far who has spoken so powerfully in this place.

We've already heard of how trauma and adverse childhood experiences can have a profound impact on people's lives, and we're already aware, of course, that that's not just through their childhood, but they can shape educational outcomes, mental health, relationships, employment and physical well-being well into adulthood. And, of course, it's very important that early intervention takes place, but we also need to ensure that there's access to the right support for people who do disclose, or are going through reliving traumatic experiences later on as an adult as well.

We heard from the Member who presented the motion that it can take, on average, for any victims of childhood sexual abuse 26 years to disclose that abuse. At that stage, someone's well into their adulthood and needs appropriate support through that. It's in that context that, last week, I had the privilege of spending time with Stepping Stones, who are based in my constituency of Fflint Wrecsam, a fantastic charity that supports adult survivors of child sexual abuse, as well as supporting their wider families, carers and friends. Seeing their work first-hand was a powerful reminder that while policy is important, it absolutely has to be done right. It's often charities and community organisations that provide the support that people rely on day to day. It is important that those organisations, whilst commissioned perhaps by public bodies, whether it's health or local authorities, in this context, it's actually really important to have organisations that sit outside of Government, in a sense, because of issues of trust that can occur at times, with services that have existed for people in the past.

It's the dedicated staff and professional counsellors at Stepping Stones who provide a safe environment and services, aiming to protect and preserve the good health, both mental and physical, of people who've been victims of sexual abuse, and in particular by the provision of therapeutic intervention and individual and group counselling. That kind of counselling and therapeutic support can make an enormous difference, not only in helping individuals in the place they're in today, but also in preventing challenges from becoming more severe and requiring more intensive public services later on down the track—something that's already been alluded to in this place this afternoon.

But, Deputy Presiding Officer, one issue they raised with me last week really stood out, and it was that, despite the vital work they do, they operate with significant uncertainty, because much of their funding is allocated on an annual basis, and people who make use of those services need to know that those services and that support are there not just for this year, but for future years as well. Long-term support is absolutely necessary. So, currently, every year, this organisation, Stepping Stones, must reapply for funding without any guarantee that it will continue. Often, decisions are not confirmed until well into the financial year, making it incredibly difficult to plan services, retain those experienced staff or invest for the future.

Cabinet Minister, I appreciate that public finances are under pressure, but organisations delivering essential trauma-informed services should not have to spend so much time worrying about whether they will still exist the following year. As I say, the people who require that support need to know that services are there into the future as well. So, I wonder, in the Cabinet Minister's response, whether she would consider whether longer term funding arrangements could be introduced for charities such as this and, on the multi-year funding where appropriate, whether that would provide greater stability, allow organisations such as Stepping Stones to plan ahead, retain those skilled counsellors and focus their time on supporting those who need them, rather than continually bidding for short-term funding grants.

If we're serious about supporting people who've gone through these adverse childhood experiences, we must be serious about providing that sustainable support for the organisations doing this work day in and day out. I'm certainly grateful to everyone at Stepping Stones for welcoming me last week and for sharing their experiences. Their passion and dedication are really clear to see, and I hope the Welsh Government will reflect on the challenges that they have highlighted. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: Funding for additional learning needs in the first Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
We are, of course, today debating the use of the additional funding for additional learning needs through the first supplementary budget. But, at its heart, this is about whether the system of funding is actually keeping pace with the reality in our schools—and I will take a moment to declare a potential interest as an LEA governor of a school in north Wales. No-one disputes the importance of ensuring children and young people with additional learning needs need to receive the support that they require. That duty is fundamental to a fair education system. But the question we must ask is whether the funding is reaching the front line in a way that reflects the scale and urgency of need today.

There is a need absolutely for a debate around sustainable funding for ALN, but we're not addressing the need that is very present today, and I wonder if this has been properly understood by the Welsh Government. We heard a few moments ago from the previous education Minister that when that money was announced, she was asking for that money to be passported through to schools for ALN. I'm not sure the education Minister now is asking the same questions of the finance Minister, whether she's banging that door for that money to go to schools here in Wales, because, across Wales, schools are under significant financial pressures as ALN demands continue to rise. They would want their Government here in Wales to ensure they are properly funded to support those children.

Headteachers and governing bodies are increasingly being forced to absorb costs within already stretched budgets, and, in many cases, schools are running deficits not because of mismanagement, but because they're having to meet statutory responsibilities without sufficient timely funding to match rising need. And instead of additional learning needs provision being fully resourced through a coherent system, the burden has been shifted onto individual schools. Staff are being asked to do more with less, and school budgets are being stretched to breaking point. That is not sustainable and it risks undermining both educational outcomes and staff retention.

Here in Wales, too often, schools are left carrying the financial risk directly, with deficits building up at school level rather than being properly managed at a system level, and I think this is where, perhaps, some of the misunderstanding has come about. We've already heard from colleagues across the Chamber that the debt sits around ALN funding at an individual school level. To say that councils will not receive the same one-off funding to write off special education debts accumulated by local government in England because those debts do not exist in Wales in the same way does not reflect the reality on the ground. Of course, most of these pressures will not appear neatly labelled as an ALN debt on a budget ledger, but they are the reason why so many schools in Wales are now running those significant deficit budgets. Schools are running tens of millions of pounds in deficits. That is a very real debt within our education system, and ALN forms a substantial part of that pressure. contributions.item_title_en: 6. Welsh Conservatives Debate: Hospital services and hospital closures
contributions.text_english:
There's clearly a health crisis in Wales. We've heard it from many Members across this Chamber so far in this debate. I was pleased to hear the previous speaker from Plaid Cymru—and I certainly appreciate his clinical experience in this field—but we've also heard so far of the experience of many people in this Chamber of broken promises. When those services have been rearranged, it often leads to that downgrading. To address the point from the Member for Plaid Cymru who spoke a moment ago, what we're calling for as Welsh Conservatives is trying to deal with that fear of ongoing future adjustments, which inevitably leads to downgrading of those services.

When I speak to my constituents in Fflint Wrecsam about healthcare in Wales, they talk about access and waiting times. People tell me it's not working as it should. It's very much the same message that I've been hearing across this Chamber so far. The Minister will know that Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board has been in special measures for a decade now. Despite the efforts and professionalism of staff on the ground, people in north Wales have faced years of pressures on services, long waiting times and real difficulty accessing care when they need it. As part of dealing with this, as an example, we are here to call on the Welsh Government to provide clear, long-term stability for our local healthcare network, specifically asking for that definitive commitment that rules out any further hospital closures or the downgrading of services. On this, I speak for the constituents of Fflint Wrecsam. They need a guarantee of that service continuity to give that confidence back into my constituency that those services are there for them in the future.

To understand why this is so important, we must see how our healthcare system is functioning on the ground. Consider the position of Wrexham Maelor Hospital. The Maelor acts as a central acute anchor for my constituents. It's no secret that the hospital is already operating at and often beyond its intended capacity. If services are downgraded or removed from surrounding areas, those patients, as the Minister understands, will not just disappear, they're simply displaced, and the vast majority will end up at the Maelor's emergency department and clinics. You cannot reduce capacity in one part of my constituency without creating an unmanageable domino effect at the main acute site at Maelor.

Sadly, we're seeing other examples of this taking place currently. I have a group of residents in Saltney Ferry who can't even register with a GP, they're not covered by a GP practice. It's a strange anomaly. Many of those in that community are now having to access primary care in England because that availability is not there for them here in Wales. What we then see, if people can't access their GP, is that they're ending up at the A&E departments. They've got nowhere else to go.

There are some other specific challenges facing my constituents in Fflint Wrecsam. Over the years, Flintshire has already experienced the loss of those community hospital beds and local minor injury provision, similar to what colleagues across the Chamber have already pointed to. That further centralisation of services away from towns and villages around Fflint Wrecsam is a regressive step. Local clinics and community beds are essential, they manage health issues early and prevent the major hospitals, especially at Wrexham Maelor, from becoming overwhelmed.

Minister, I would say that geography and infrastructure must support healthcare policy, not just administrative convenience. Of course, our proximity in Fflint Wrexham to the English border means that any reduction in Welsh NHS capacity risks putting more pressure on those cross-border services, complicating care pathways for patients that I represent.

Finally, Llywydd, I want to mention hospice and palliative care. This is some of the most important work in the entire health system. While not necessarily directly funded for all the services they provide, they are vital facilities, taking significant pressure off directly funded NHS services. I spent some time again last week with Nightingale House Hospice in my constituency, and it's clear to see the incredible work they and hospices across Wales do for patients and families at the hardest times in their lives. They provide dignity, comfort and support when people need it most. But we've already seen in north Wales vital services in hospice and palliative care being cut back due to funding not being enough. I continue to hear from hospices their concerns about funding and long-term stability. We do not want to see those facilities being withdrawn in Wales, and particularly in the area I represent. If we say we value dignity in healthcare, then hospice care has to be properly supported so it can continue to deliver those vital services that people in Wales need.

In closing, Llywydd, I want to see certainty and security in healthcare. We need an explicit commitment to maintain our current hospital services, protect our local beds and invest sustainably in the healthcare infrastructure here in Wales. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: The First Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement and for your early engagement on this supplementary budget.

Of course, this first supplementary budget gives the new Welsh Government an important opportunity to set out its priorities. When people look at this budget, they are thinking about the issues that affect their daily lives, their jobs, their business, their local school or hospital, and whether they feel confident about the future. They want reassurance that the Government they elected last month will make decisions that will help improve their lives, create opportunities for the next generation, and deliver value for hard-working taxpayers.

We know, then, that the first question to enable this is whether the supplementary budget does enough to support growth in our Welsh economy. A strong economy creates jobs, supports enterprise, attracts investment and generates the revenue needed to fund and sustainably invest in our vital public services, and most importantly enables people to get on, flourish and pull themselves away from poverty.

Businesses across Wales regularly tell me that they want a Welsh Government that understands the importance of growth. They want investment in infrastructure, better transport links, and policies that encourage them to expand, innovate and create jobs. We need to know how the Government intends to support enterprise, attract investment and create the conditions for businesses to succeed. Indeed, in the 'The First 100 Days' document from Plaid Cymru, it is stated that:

'Our economic plan will unlock that potential—growing and sustaining Welsh-owned businesses, delivering good jobs, reviving our town centres and boosting living standards.'

It is a surprise, then, Cabinet Minister, that this supplementary budget seems to look like a missed opportunity to address even slightly some of those issues in the economy. Can the Cabinet Minister explain specifically how the measures contained within this supplementary budget will help deliver that objective of an improved economy? This question is particularly important given that Wales continues to face long-standing economic challenges after nearly 27 years of a Labour-led Government. Economic growth has too often lagged behind other parts of the UK, leading to disproportionate levels of poverty here in Wales.

I am concerned, Cabinet Minister, that your initial approach does seem to be dealing with the symptoms and not the cause. You have announced, of course, the £2 million of Cynnal funding, which is essentially welfare spend, which is not a devolved remit. How will you ensure that this is best value for money for Welsh taxpayers, and achieve sustained, transformative growth in our economy—the compassionate approach that we need—rather than causing more people to get stuck in a cycle of poverty?

On education, Cabinet Minister, parents and teachers across Wales want well-funded schools, supported by a funding formula that is fair and fit for purpose. I welcome the additional capital funding for school maintenance, but I will join colleagues in this place in regard to the ALN funding. I think there’s a misunderstanding of where the debt sits around ALN funding. You said in your statement that you

'spoke to the leader of local government...last week to explain that councils will not receive the one-off funding to write off special education debts accumulated by local government in England, as those debts do not exist in Wales in the same way.'

Of course, most of those debts won't show as an ALN debt on a budget ledger. They are the reason, often, why so many schools in Wales now are running deficit budgets. Schools in Wales are running tens of millions of pounds in deficit budgets. That is the very real debt that education and schools are in, and ALN is a significant proportion of that.

That has to be recognised, Cabinet Minister. I’m not sure what your officials are telling you if you think that that debt does not exist here in Wales. It definitely does, and it needs to be addressed. And I would expect that there's a fair argument to recognise this and to provide one-off funding to alleviate these deficits and then use the future funding that you're going to get, as you said, in 2028, to put a sustainable model in place. I absolutely agree with you that there has to be a sustainable model, but you also have to address the deficit that has been caused over recent years. So, would you commit to investigating this further and seeing whether that is an approach that could be acceptable?

I'll briefly touch on healthcare, Cabinet Minister. We're grateful, of course, for the dedication and professionalism of NHS staff across Wales, yet patients continue to face significant challenges, including those long waiting times. It's welcome to see your supplementary budget seeking to address some of those issues in the short term, but as Darren Miller mentioned earlier, there's a risk that an unsustainable model is being created that isn't necessarily best value for money. So, how will you ensure that you're getting the best bang for your buck when it comes to that £100 million investment in health services, and how will you ensure that this spend is going to create good value for money?

contributions.text_english:
I think it's absolutely right for Members of this place to ask for assurances from its Government as to the safeguarding arrangements that are in place for any type of people across our country, because safeguarding our communities is a fundamental role of all elected Members in this place.

The First Minister will be aware that one of the biggest safeguarding scandals of our time has been that of the grooming gangs seen across the UK, and it shows what happens when authorities fail to ask difficult questions or to properly investigate concerns: victims being let down. We have a duty to make sure that those mistakes never are repeated. That's why I'm disappointed that Plaid Cymru has refused to back a Wales-wide grooming gangs inquiry. At a time when survivors are asking for answers, surely we should be looking at those issues more closely, not shutting down further scrutiny. So, if the Welsh Government is confident that safeguarding measures are working across Wales, why won't it support a Wales-wide inquiry to help give victims the answers they deserve and reassure the public that lessons have been learned?

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language: Priorities for Education
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for your statement, and for sharing it in advance also, and for your early engagement. I declare an interest as an LEA governor as well. I agree with you, Cabinet Minister, that education should be giving every young person in Wales the best possible start in life, but parents across Wales are all asking the same question: is this system delivering the standards our children deserve? And unfortunately, the answer right now to that question is 'no'; the system is not delivering the standards our children deserve. The fact is that we are spending more per head in Wales than in England, yet outcomes continue to lag behind.

So, I wonder, as my first question, Cabinet Minister, if you have a view as to the biggest reason why there continues to be a gap, despite that sustained investment over time. It's not enough to point to increased spending; we have to be honest about whether that money is translating into better outcomes for learners. And you've rightly pointed to the desired focus on standards. The reality is that we continue to see Wales at or near the bottom of UK education rankings, and consistently doing poorly on international PISA rankings, with too many young people still leaving school without secure literacy and numeracy skills. That's a long-standing issue and one that requires urgent attention and clear accountability. And in particular, on those PISA rankings, I wonder if you have a target in mind as to where you want Wales to be at the end of this Senedd term to show progress in relation to all-important standards, and also a position that you want to be held accountable for in terms of those PISA rankings.

Attendance remains below that of pre-pandemic levels—I agree with you that there has to be a focus on attendance—falling from 94 per cent to around 91 per cent currently. For some of the most vulnerable learners, particularly those eligible for free school meals, persistent absence remains far too high. So, I wonder what further action will be taken to engage with parents to drive up attendance and ensure consistency across all schools, particularly for those disadvantaged pupils.

We're also, as we've heard, seeing pressures on the system itself. We know that teacher numbers and support staff numbers have fallen in recent years, while demands on schools have increased. And Cabinet Minister, you mentioned the new teacher initiative of £20,000 to encourage new teachers into the system. But you'll also know that, in England, new teachers are offered £30,000 to start teaching. So, I wonder how you think you'll address that gap of £30,000 to start teaching in England but £20,000 to start teaching here in Wales.

On mobile phones in schools, this has been an issue raised consistently by teachers and headteachers, and by the Welsh Conservatives in this Chamber as well. And new survey findings published today by the Welsh Conservatives also reinforce this concern, showing mobile phone restrictions are widely seen as having positive impacts on reducing distraction, improving behaviour, tackling bullying and supporting learner well-being. I welcome your statement, your commitment, to consult on statutory guidance to limit mobile phone use in schools. But can you confirm today whether the Welsh Government intends to take a more consistent, national approach to mobile phone use in schools, or whether it will continue to leave these decisions entirely to individual schools without a national framework in place?

You acknowledged, Cabinet Minister, the importance of higher education to the Welsh economy, and indeed Lynne Neagle also picked up on this point, because it, of course, helps create jobs and growth. However, we know that fewer students are going to university here in Wales than in England, which is putting pressure on universities and how they are funded. I believe if we connect universities, apprenticeships and the needs of the economy more closely, we can keep higher education strong, make it more accessible and ensure it's financially sustainable in the long term. But I'd be keen to hear your views on the future of the sector. I appreciate you've answered that, in part, to Lynne Neagle a moment ago, but I would be keen to hear that in a little more detail, to give that assurance to our higher education providers.

Deputy Presiding Officer, this is a system that the new Welsh Government has inherited, a system with clear and persistent challenges, so the question that needs answering now is not linked to blame, but about direction and outcomes. Because, ultimately, people will judge this Welsh Government not on plans or statements, but on whether things actually improve in the classroom, and, in my role in this place, that's what I will continue to do to scrutinise your decisions. Diolch yn fawr iawn.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you for your response, Cabinet Minister. You'll know the important role that faith groups have in education here in Wales, in particular both the Catholic Church and the Church in Wales, in having schools all across Wales. In my part of the world in Fflint Wrecsam, the Catholic Church has a number of schools in some of our poorest areas, in some of our most needy areas, and do a fantastic job in supporting our communities.

You may be aware that Flintshire County Council are pursuing an agenda of closing a number of these Catholic schools in my area, specifically in Saltney, where St Anthony's Catholic Primary School is under threat of closure. Secondly, would you be willing to meet with me to discuss this issue further to see what solutions may be available?

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Reform UK Debate: Childcare offer
contributions.text_english:
I'm grateful to have the opportunity to speak in today's debate. I want to try and attempt to answer a question as to why this motion today is so important. Because, for me, this debate is not just about pounds, shillings and pence, but rather about a message to parents and families around confidence in starting or growing a family. And western societies, like ours here in Wales, are facing a crisis, and that's one of declining birth rates. While it's perhaps not something we debate often in this Chamber, it will become one of the defining issues of our age that will impact every aspect of society. We currently have a declining birth rate at a level of 1.44 children being born per couple, well below the 2.1 required to maintain population levels as they are. This continued trajectory will create severe challenges for public services, the workforce and economic growth, and childcare costs and associated pressures are repeatedly shown to be a major factor in this trend.

Of course, childcare is one of the most important areas of public policy, because it sits at the intersection of family life and economic opportunity. It affects how families organise their lives, whether parents can work, and how children are supported in their earliest and most formative years. When childcare is affordable and flexible, parents are able to participate fully in the workforce, businesses benefit from more stable labour supply, and the wider economy becomes more productive. When it’s expensive or inflexible, it can become a barrier to work and place additional pressure on family finances. But childcare is much more than just economics alone; it’s about supporting families to make the right choices that are right for them and their children. Any successful childcare system must recognise the realities of family life and provide parents with genuine flexibility. That is why getting childcare policy right requires more than just ambition: it requires clarity about what is being proposed, how it will be delivered and how it will be paid for, so that families can have certainty and confidence to plan and prepare for the future.

If a policy is genuinely affordable, then publishing those full costings should strengthen confidence in it, not weaken it. If it is not, then the public deserves to understand what choices are being made elsewhere in the budget to pay for it. The debate is not simply about cost, it is about the broader policy—the kind of childcare system we want to see here in Wales. Welsh Conservatives believe childcare policy should be designed around families, not around Government. Government, of course, has an important enabling role in helping parents balance work and caring responsibilities, but it should do so in a way that recognises the different circumstances and choices of families across Wales, because while the state can create the right environments for children to be raised, it should never replace the role of the family. Parents remain at the centre of a child’s life, supported by grandparents, relatives and wider family networks, whose contributions remain invaluable to working families and communities alike.

That reality is already visible across Wales. Many families rely not on a single model of childcare, but on a combination of formal provision and informal family support. A successful childcare system should recognise that diversity, strengthen it and give parents the flexibility to choose the arrangements that work best for them and their children. Because, ultimately, a strong childcare system is about trust: trust in families to make decisions about their own lives, and trust in Government to be honest about what funding its policies will require to deliver its policies. That is why a policy like this should be properly costed, properly planned and properly transparent from the outset. This gives families confidence in starting—

contributions.item_title_en: 6. Welsh Labour Debate: School support staff negotiating body
contributions.text_english:
I too must declare an interest as a local education authority governor of a school in north Wales. School staff are so important to our education system here in Wales. Teaching assistants, catering staff, cleaners, caretakers and administrative workers keep our schools running every single day. They're essential to the learning environment, even if their contribution is not always visible in the same way as classroom teaching. Yet, for too long, their pay, conditions and recognition have not reflected their importance. We've already heard, haven't we, how many are employed on term-time-only contracts, meaning they are, effectively, paid for around nine months of the year rather than 12, which creates financial insecurity in work. These are almost already the lowest paid in the public sector, and it's felt most sharply by those with the least flexibility to absorb it.

There is also inconsistency built into the current system. Pay and conditions can vary from one local authority to another quite significantly, even for staff doing very much the same roles. That means recognition and reward for their work depends too heavily on where they happen to be employed, rather than the value of what they do.

But, Deputy Presiding Officer, we have to be honest about how we got here. This is not a new problem. It's been developed over 27 years of Labour in government here in Wales, propped up by Plaid Cymru, during which these structural issues in our education workforce were allowed to persist. Staff have been left in a system that's fragmented, under pressure and increasingly reliant on goodwill rather than proper structure. It's therefore not credible for those same parties to now present themselves as discovering these problems for the first time or to claim ownership of a solution only once they are no longer solely responsible for fixing it.

We also know the system is under pressure. Workforce data shows that the number of learning support workers has declined in recent years. Schools are reporting growing strain on staffing and increasing reliance on support staff to fill gaps where teachers are absent. That is not a sustainable position for any education system. It's in this context that the proposal for a statutory school support staff negotiating body does become important. The principle is to bring structure where there's been fragmentation and consistency where there's been variation. Where a workforce is as large and vital as this one, there should be a proper mechanism for negotiating pay and conditions, rather than leaving it for uneven local arrangements.

This is about fairness, but it's also about stability. Schools function best when staff feel valued, secure and properly supported. When support staff face insecurity in pay and limited progression, it affects retention, morale and, ultimately, the quality of support available to pupils in the classroom. We agree that a statutory negotiating body would give school support staff a formal voice, ensure their contribution is properly recognised and help create a more coherent system across Wales. It would also help address long-standing inconsistencies that have built up over time rather than being properly resolved.

So, while this proposal is being brought forward now, it speaks of problems that have been present for many years. The question is whether we are prepared to fix those structural issues in a meaningful way, or whether we continue with a system that has clearly struggled to deliver fairness and consistency for the workforce that our schools, and, ultimately, our children, depend on. For those reasons, this proposal deserves serious consideration and support. Diolch yn fawr iawn.
